S043.name: Restrictive_Intake
S043.description: Persistent restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight.

subtypes.Eating Very Small Amounts: Eating only one or two bites a day or extremely small portions per meal.
subtypes.Skipping Meals: Intentionally skipping breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
subtypes.Exclusion of Specific Food Groups: Strictly avoiding specific food groups like carbohydrates or fats to prevent nutritional imbalance.
subtypes.Strict Calorie Restriction: Limiting daily caloric intake to an extremely low level.

S044.name: Low_Weight
S044.description: A body weight that is significantly below the minimum level of health for age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health.

subtypes.Continuous Weight Loss: A state where weight continues to decrease due to intentional restriction of intake.
subtypes.Insistence on Low Weight: Attempting to lose more weight or refusing to restore weight despite already being underweight.

S045.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
S045.description: Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, even though at a significantly low weight.

subtypes.Fear of Weight Gain: Extreme fear and loathing of gaining weight or becoming fat.
subtypes.Fear of Specific Foods: Fear that eating high-calorie foods will immediately lead to weight gain.
subtypes.Obsession with Weight Gain: Compulsively checking the scale and becoming extremely anxious about even the slightest increase.

S046.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
S046.description: Undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.

subtypes.Distorted Body Image: Perceiving one's body as much fatter than it actually is or perceiving specific parts as excessively large when looking in the mirror.
subtypes.Self-Worth Dependent on Weight: Judging whether one is a good or successful person solely based on weight or body shape.

S084.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
S084.description: Persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

subtypes.Denial of Medical Risk: Not admitting or dismissing the health risks caused by being underweight.
subtypes.Disregard of Symptoms: Not taking physical symptoms caused by low weight (dizziness, hair loss, amenorrhea) seriously.
subtypes.Dismissal of Concerns: Exaggerating or rejecting the concerns of doctors or family as unnecessary.

symptom.disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced or evaluated. Individuals often exhibit rigid control over food, exercise, and body-related routines, with a strong link between self-worth and thinness, and may deny the seriousness of their low weight despite medical compromise. Onset is most common in adolescence or young adulthood, but it can emerge or recur later in life, often in the context of stress, role transitions, or situations that heighten focus on appearance or control. The course can be chronic or relapsing, distinguishing it from transient dieting or weight loss due to medical illness or other psychiatric conditions, and it requires careful differentiation from other eating and body image disorders such as bulimia nervosa and body dysmorphic disorder.

patient.stressor: Jaritza’s eating problems began to take shape when her warehouse introduced a new productivity tracking system that ranked workers by output and error rates on a public dashboard. Around the same time, she was passed over for an internal promotion to logistics coordinator, with a supervisor hinting that the role demanded someone who could "present more professionally" in front of clients, which she privately interpreted as a criticism of her appearance. Wanting to prove she was disciplined enough for the next opening, she started tightening up her routines—getting to work early, taking fewer breaks, and gradually trimming back her meals on shift to stay "light" and energized. Over several months, coworkers at the Midstate Trailblazers hiking club and at church potlucks began commenting with concern about how little she was eating and how much smaller she looked, and when dizziness on the warehouse floor led to a near-fainting episode at work, her manager insisted she see a doctor, who then referred her for psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: I’ve gotten so strict about cutting back how much I eat that I hardly feel like I’m taking in anything at all anymore.

patient.stressor: For Donald, the shift from steady contractor work to trying to build his own mural business brought a mix of exhilaration and chronic financial strain, with irregular income, late-paying clients, and mounting credit card debt for supplies and travel to art festivals. As money became tighter, he told himself he was "too busy painting to eat" and that skipping meals was a smart way to save time and cash, gradually turning food into something he felt he needed to control as tightly as his budgets and color palettes. Long days on scaffolding with little more than coffee left him increasingly depleted, yet he took pride in how little he was spending on groceries, even as friends in his hiking group and at open-mic nights remarked on how drawn and fragile he looked. When a minor fall from a ladder led to an urgent care visit and the medical team expressed alarm at his low weight and recent history, he was advised to seek specialized psychiatric care for an eating disorder.
patient.chief_complaint: People keep saying I’m way too thin and need help, but I honestly don’t see what the big problem is with my weight being this low.

patient.stressor: Tam’s difficulties around eating intensified in her early forties, as she navigated a cluster of transitions: her teenage children becoming more independent, her parents in Trinidad and Tobago needing more long-distance support, and a promotion at the fabrication plant that moved her from hands-on work to a more visible supervisory role. Feeling caught between caregiving expectations, leadership responsibilities, and the youth-focused culture of her multicultural choir and dance groups, she became increasingly preoccupied with presenting a lean, "ageless" image. She began staying late at the shop and skipping shared meals at home to "get more done," while also ramping up her jogging and yoga, telling herself she was just committing to wellness as life got more demanding. When her choir director and a close friend from her art collective separately expressed worry about how gaunt she looked and how often she declined the elaborate meals she used to love cooking, her husband encouraged her to see their primary care physician, whose concerns about her weight loss led to a psychiatric referral.
patient.chief_complaint: Lately I feel like how my body looks and what I weigh are all I can focus on when I think about whether I’m doing well in life.
